**Cameroon General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 2 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2025. Duration: three hours.**

Instructions to candidates: Answer FIVE questions, choosing AT LEAST TWO from each section. All questions carry equal marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

Q5(a) imprime « (5+5 marks) » pour (i) et (ii) et Q6(b) « (5+5+5 marks) » pour (i), (ii), (iii) : ces points sont regroupés dans la sous-question (10 et 15). Aucun écart constaté entre les points imprimés.

Sujet scanné (filigrane gcerevision.com en travers des pages, sans conséquence sur la lisibilité) ; aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées, les chiffres des exemples (FCFA, quantités, taux) sont hypothétiques et recalculés avec Python ; aucune statistique réelle n'est avancée. Les repères institutionnels cités (BEAC, franc CFA arrimé à l'euro) relèvent de la culture générale, pas du sujet.

Les questions de la Section B sont numérotées 5 à 8 (pas de renumérotation « B1 »). Le sujet tient en deux pages (page de garde et questions) : aucune question n'est coupée ni illisible.

questions.enonce_markdown:
What are the differences between tariffs and quotas?

(8 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** Tariffs and quotas are the two main **barriers to trade** used to protect domestic industries from foreign competition, but they work in different ways.

- A **tariff** (customs duty) is a **tax on imported goods**, either **specific** (a fixed amount per unit) or **ad valorem** (a percentage of the value).
- A **quota** is a **physical limit on the quantity (or value)** of a good that may be imported in a given period.

**Differences.**

1. **Nature.** A tariff is a **tax (price-based)** measure; a quota is a **quantity-based** (non-price) restriction.
2. **How it restricts imports.** A tariff raises the price of imports and so **reduces the quantity indirectly**; a quota fixes the quantity directly and the price rises because the supply is limited.
3. **Certainty of the effect.** With a quota the quantity of imports is **certain** (it cannot exceed the limit); with a tariff the quantity imported is **uncertain**, because it depends on the elasticity of demand and on whether foreign firms cut their price to absorb the tax.
4. **Revenue.** A tariff **brings revenue to the government**; a quota brings **no revenue**, unless import licences are auctioned. Otherwise the higher price gives a **windfall profit (quota rent)** to the importers or the licence holders, or to foreign producers.
5. **Administration.** A tariff is **simple** to apply at the border; a quota requires a **licensing system**, which is more costly to administer and open to **bribery and corruption**.
6. **Reaction to changes in demand.** Under a tariff, if demand rises, more is imported at the higher price; under a quota, if demand rises, imports remain fixed and the **price rises further**.
7. **Competition.** A tariff lets foreign producers who are efficient enough to pay it continue to compete; a quota guarantees a market share to domestic producers and may create **monopoly power** for the producers who have the right to import.
8. **International rules.** Tariffs are the form of protection generally allowed (and negotiated down) in the framework of the World Trade Organisation and regional agreements, while quotas are more restricted.

**Numerical illustration (hypothetical).** Suppose the world price of a good is 1 000 FCFA per unit. A tariff of 200 FCFA per unit raises the domestic price to 1 200 FCFA. If 45 units are still imported, the government collects $200 \times 45 = 9\,000$ FCFA. A quota of 45 units would give the same domestic price and quantity, but the 9 000 FCFA would go to the holders of the import licences, not to the government.

**Conclusion.** A tariff is a tax which works through the price and raises revenue; a quota limits the quantity directly and gives certainty about the volume of imports but no revenue and more scope for corruption.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Examine the negative effects of tariffs.

(12 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction.** A tariff is a tax on imports, used to protect domestic firms, raise revenue or improve the balance of payments. It has, however, many **negative effects**.

1. **Higher prices and a loss of consumer surplus.** Imported goods cost more, and domestic producers can also raise their prices under the shelter of the tariff. Consumers, especially low-income households, pay more and the **real income falls**.
2. **Reduced choice and quality.** Fewer imported varieties are available, and protected firms have less incentive to maintain quality.
3. **Inefficiency and misallocation of resources.** The protected industry is shielded from competition, so it may remain **inefficient and costly**; resources are drawn into the production of goods in which the country has a **comparative disadvantage**. This produces a **deadweight loss** (a net loss of welfare).
4. **Retaliation and trade wars.** Other countries may impose tariffs in return, reducing **exports**, output and employment in the country's export industries (for example cocoa or timber exporters).
5. **Higher costs for domestic firms that use imported inputs.** A tariff on raw materials, spare parts or machinery raises production costs and makes the country's own exports **less competitive**.
6. **Fall in the volume of international trade and in the gains from specialisation.** Countries lose the benefits of the international division of labour and of larger markets.
7. **Smuggling, corruption and evasion.** High tariffs encourage smuggling and under-invoicing, which reduces revenue and rewards dishonest traders.
8. **Uncertain revenue.** If the tariff is effective in cutting imports, the revenue it brings falls; a government that depends on customs duties has an unstable budget.
9. **A possible rise in the price level.** Dearer imports and inputs add to **cost-push inflation**.
10. **Protection may never end.** "Infant" industries may become dependent on protection, and the tariff may be defended by the interests of the protected firms and workers.
11. **Conflict with regional and international commitments.** In a customs union or free-trade area (CEMAC, the African Continental Free Trade Area, WTO rules), national tariffs may break agreements and may slow regional integration.
12. **Harm to poorer countries and consumers.** Tariffs imposed by rich countries on the goods of poorer countries lower their export earnings.

**Numerical illustration (hypothetical).** The world price is 1 000 FCFA. A tariff of 200 FCFA per unit (20 percent) raises the domestic price to 1 200 FCFA: domestic output rises from 40 to 55 units, domestic demand falls from 120 to 100 units, and imports fall from 80 to 45 units. Then:
- loss of consumer surplus $= 200 \times 100 + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 200 \times 20 = 22\,000$ FCFA;
- gain of domestic producers $= 200 \times 40 + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 200 \times 15 = 9\,500$ FCFA;
- government revenue $= 200 \times 45 = 9\,000$ FCFA;
- **deadweight loss** $= \tfrac{1}{2} \times 200 \times 15 + \tfrac{1}{2} \times 200 \times 20 = 3\,500$ FCFA, and $9\,500 + 9\,000 + 3\,500 = 22\,000$.

*Diagram (to be drawn in the exam).* Domestic demand $D$ and supply $S$, the world price line $P_w$ and the higher line $P_w + t$. The loss of consumer surplus is the area between the two price lines under $D$; it is divided into the producers' gain, the government revenue (the rectangle between the lines over the remaining imports) and the **two small triangles of deadweight loss**.

**Conclusion.** Tariffs raise prices, shelter inefficiency, invite retaliation and reduce the gains from trade. They are justified only in limited cases (infant industries, national security, revenue); in general their costs to consumers and to the economy outweigh the benefits.
